module_title: DNS, Route 53 and Hybrid Name Resolution
review_basis: Individually inspected approved SAP module 05 WebPs slides 13–15; diagrams, labels, policy decisions, alternatives and caveats drive each narration.
part_title: Hybrid PrivateLink DNS, DNS Firewall and Resolver Evidence

scenes.title: Hybrid PrivateLink: DNS and connection use separate paths
scenes.visual_overview: Two panels place the corporate DNS query to a Resolver inbound endpoint on the left and the actual application connection to a PrivateLink ENI on the right.
visual_walkthrough: Follow corporate client and conditional DNS forwarder to the inbound endpoint
Trace the private DNS answer that returns an interface endpoint ENI private IP
Follow the separate application TLS connection over VPN or Direct Connect to the ENI security-group boundary
Explain central endpoint placement, avoiding static ENI IPs and separate DNS versus network troubleshooting
scenes.visual_example: An on-premises client resolves an AWS private API name over Route 53 Resolver but still needs its own routed TCP 443 path to the interface endpoint.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A valid private DNS answer cannot substitute for a functioning network route and authorized endpoint connection.
scenes.narration: This slide deliberately splits the process in two. First examine the cyan DNS path on the left. A corporate client asks corporate DNS for a service name. The configured conditional forwarder sends that query to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint inside the endpoint VPC. If private DNS is supported and configured, the VPC Resolver provides the appropriate private interface endpoint address. The resolver's role ends with returning the DNS answer. Now shift to the purple application path on the right. The corporate client uses the resolved private IP and connects through VPN or Direct Connect, actual network routing, and the interface endpoint security group on the service port, such as TCP four four three. The endpoint then presents the published PrivateLink service. Review the four lower callouts. The inbound Resolver endpoint must have the correct private DNS view. Interface endpoints may be centralized, but routing to their private addresses remains necessary. Clients should not hardcode ENI IP addresses, since endpoint configuration can change. Finally, troubleshoot name resolution and traffic connectivity separately. DNS never acts as the proxy for this application data path.

scenes.title: DNS Firewall: control domain resolution
scenes.visual_overview: VPC and hybrid workloads query AmazonProvidedDNS, then DNS Firewall evaluates associated rule groups and domain lists before allowing or blocking the DNS answer.
visual_walkthrough: Trace supported DNS queries through the VPC Resolver toward DNS Firewall
Inspect ordered rule groups and lower numeric rule priorities, plus custom and managed domain lists
Compare approved domain answer with blocked NXDOMAIN, NODATA or override response
Read fail-open/closed behavior, query logs, test cases and encrypted-DNS limitations
scenes.visual_example: A security team blocks a suspicious domain for VPC workloads via Resolver DNS Firewall, while application traffic that bypasses that resolver still requires egress controls.
scenes.visual_synthesis: DNS Firewall is a domain resolution control, not a universal network packet firewall.
scenes.narration: Start with the workloads on the left: EC2, EKS and a hybrid client using the VPC Resolver. DNS Firewall applies to supported DNS requests processed by that resolver. Follow the arrow into the central firewall block. Multiple associated rule groups are evaluated in their configured order, and rules within a group use numeric priorities. Domain lists can be organization-defined or AWS managed. Continue to the right: an approved name resolves normally, whereas a blocked name returns the configured block response, such as NXDOMAIN, NODATA or a supported override. The six numbered lower sections help with real deployment. Confirm rule group association order and rule actions such as allow, block and alert. Maintain appropriate domain lists. Choose fail-open or fail-closed behavior deliberately for cases when DNS Firewall cannot answer. Enable query logging and alarms to investigate decisions. Test the expected blocked response. Most important, understand the scope: traffic that uses other DNS mechanisms, including some encrypted DNS paths, may bypass the VPC Resolver. Domain policy is a defense layer. Pair it with appropriate routing, egress and application controls rather than assuming every network flow is inspected.

scenes.title: Resolver query logs: evidence with limits
scenes.visual_overview: A VPC DNS client and Route 53 Resolver feed a regional query logging configuration, which delivers data to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose; an example record sits at right.
visual_walkthrough: Trace the DNS request from client into Resolver and its regional logging configuration
Compare CloudWatch Logs, S3 and Kinesis Data Firehose destinations
Read the example source IP, name, type, response code, timestamp, answers and DNS Firewall action
Explain resolver caching gaps, permission requirements and correlation with other operational evidence
scenes.visual_example: A security analyst sees no recent Resolver query entry for api.example.com, but the client may have reused a cached answer.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Resolver query logs show selected resolution activity, not a complete list of client lookups or packet captures.
scenes.narration: This slide focuses on what Route 53 Resolver query logs actually show. On the left a VPC client sends a DNS question to Resolver. A regional query logging configuration, associated with the relevant VPC, delivers eligible query records to the destinations in the middle: CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Kinesis Data Firehose. On the right, inspect the sample record. It includes the source IP, queried name, DNS record type, response code, timestamp, returned answers, and potentially a DNS Firewall decision. Those fields help identify what was resolved and whether a policy applied. But the bottom-left warning is essential. Resolver query logging does not necessarily record every application lookup: cached answers may not produce another Resolver-processed query record. Therefore an absent log entry is a clue, not proof that no lookup occurred. The middle panel reminds us to configure the logging resource in the correct Region and grant destination permissions. The right panel tells us to correlate DNS responses with network reachability and application logs. Resolver query logs are not packet captures and must not be confused with public hosted zone query logging.
